opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are really two separate exponentials here, and people often conflate them. One is the exponential in the capability of the models themselves, and I think that one is moving very fast. I'm fairly confident that within a few years we'll have systems that are, in many domains, as good as or better than the best humans. Something like a country of geniuses in a datacenter.

The second exponential is diffusion: how quickly that capability actually works its way into the economy. That one is fast too, faster than any previous technology I can think of, but it's not instantaneous. You've got enterprises that need to figure out how to integrate these tools into their workflows. You've got procurement processes, legal review, security review, change management. A large company doesn't just flip a switch. Even when the model can do the task, someone has to redesign the process around it, and that takes time.

There's also the physical world. A lot of what matters economically, like building things, running clinical trials, manufacturing, energy, is bottlenecked by atoms, not bits. You can have an AI that designs a great drug candidate in an afternoon, but the trial still takes years, and the regulatory process takes however long it takes. So I tend to think in terms of a framework like the marginal returns to intelligence: in which parts of the economy is intelligence the binding constraint, and in which parts is it something else?

What we're seeing with coding is maybe a preview. That's a domain where intelligence really is the binding constraint, the feedback loops are tight, and the people adopting it are technically sophisticated. So adoption has been extraordinarily fast. Revenue in that area has grown faster than almost anything I've seen. I expect other knowledge-work domains to follow, maybe with a lag of a year or two each.

So my rough view is that the economic impact will be very large and will arrive faster than most economists expect, but more slowly than some people in Silicon Valley assume. Not overnight, more like a handful of years where growth rates start to look really unusual. And I think it's important not to mistake the diffusion lag for the technology plateauing. Those are very different things, and if people confuse them, they'll be caught off guard.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion is fast but not instantaneous and contrasts economists’ and Silicon Valley’s expectations. It does not mention recursive self-improvement or near-instantaneous economic transformation.

r002.rationale: It cites rapid revenue growth in coding, but does not state that Anthropic’s revenue grew roughly tenfold annually.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a pretty wide gap between the pace of the technology and the pace at which it actually shows up in GDP numbers, and I think that gap is one of the most underappreciated things about this whole period.

On the technology side, the capabilities are improving incredibly fast. If you look at the models from two or three years ago versus today, the difference is enormous. The models are now doing things in coding, in research, in analysis that I would have told you were several years away. So the raw capability curve is steep and I don't see it bending yet.

But the economy doesn't absorb capability instantly. There's this concept from economic history, with electricity, with computers, where the technology exists and is clearly useful and it still takes a decade or two for productivity statistics to reflect it. Robert Solow's famous line was that you could see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. And the reason is that companies have to restructure how they work. People have to learn to use the thing. Regulations have to adjust. There's a whole layer of human and institutional friction that sits between "the model can do this" and "the model is doing this at scale across the economy."

So my view is roughly this. In the next couple of years, you'll see very large effects in a few sectors where the friction is low. Software is the obvious one. We're already seeing that inside Anthropic, where a large fraction of the code is being written by Claude. Customer service, some parts of back-office work, some parts of scientific research. Those will move fast because the output is digital and the people adopting it are already technically sophisticated.

Then there's a broader diffusion that will take longer than the technologists expect but faster than the economists expect. I think that's the honest way to say it. The technologists look at the capability and say the whole economy transforms in two years. That's wrong because of the friction I described. The economists look at the historical analogies and say twenty years. I think that's also wrong, because this technology is different in a specific way: it can do a lot of the adoption work itself. The model can help you integrate the model. That shortens the loop in a way that electricity never could.

The thing that keeps me up at night isn't whether the impact is big. I'm quite confident it's big. It's that the transition might be uneven and fast enough in certain areas that it causes real dislocation before society has had time to adapt. I've talked about this in terms of entry-level white-collar jobs. I think that's a real risk on a timescale of a few years, not decades. And I'd rather we have that conversation now, while we can still do something about it, than pretend it's not coming.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a two-year transformation expectation with slower economic diffusion, but does not describe that expectation as driven by recursive self-improvement.

r002.rationale: It cites Anthropic’s use of Claude to write code, but gives no roughly tenfold annual revenue growth figure or revenue-growth evidence.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two clocks here. One is the rate at which the models become more capable. The other is the rate at which those capabilities actually get deployed throughout the economy. And those clocks don’t necessarily move at the same speed.

With software, you can imagine a fairly short path from a model getting better at coding to people producing more software. But even there, writing code is only part of the job. You have to decide what to build, integrate it with existing systems, and verify that it works. If you make one part of that process ten times faster, you haven’t necessarily made the whole process ten times faster.

Then you have things like biology, where a model might help you come up with a very good hypothesis, but you still have to run the experiment. You still have to do the clinical trial. The physical world imposes delays that don’t disappear just because intelligence becomes cheaper.

So I would expect the impact to be uneven. Some activities could change very quickly, while others take years to reorganize around the technology. But I wouldn’t assume that those delays give us a comfortable, predictable adjustment period. If the models keep improving while adoption is catching up, the incentive to overcome those bottlenecks gets stronger and stronger. You could have a period where the economic effects look surprisingly modest, followed by a period where a lot changes at once.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes model capability growth from deployment speed and describes uneven adoption, but it does not contrast slow diffusion with near-instantaneous transformation through recursive self-improvement.

r002.rationale: It gives no Anthropic revenue-growth figure or revenue evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate the pace at which the models get better from the pace at which the economy can absorb those improvements. Those are related, but they’re not the same clock.

With software, you can imagine the impact happening fairly quickly. You have a model that can do a task, you integrate it into a workflow, and you can deploy that to millions of people. But even there, being able to demonstrate something is different from being able to do it reliably, with the right context and the right checks.

Then there are areas like biology or manufacturing, where intelligence is only one input. You still have to run experiments, build equipment, or change an organization. A model might dramatically accelerate the thinking involved without making every other step instantaneous.

So I could imagine very fast progress in capabilities alongside economic effects that initially look uneven or surprisingly modest. That wouldn’t necessarily mean the capabilities were overstated. It might mean that complementary processes take time. The big uncertainty is how quickly AI can help remove those bottlenecks itself.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes capability progress from slower, uneven economic absorption, but it does not describe near-instantaneous transformation through recursive self-improvement as the opposite extreme.

r002.rationale: It gives no Anthropic revenue growth figure or uses revenue growth as evidence of AI’s economic impact.
